THE CYCLE PULSE — Y3C8 The Bay Tribune — Oakland Narrated by Mags Corliss, Editor-in-Chief ============================================================ Cycle 112 opened clear after two gray ones, and you could hear the city exhale in the reporting. Noah Tan found Derlik Green taking the long way down Broadway, lingering at the light, nodding at the crew at SpeedyBurger without checking the time. Xavier Ramington in Temescal said the sun didn't change his morning, only made the familiar warmer. Then there was Brian Adams in Jack London, standing in the strip of light by the radiator just long enough to warm his hands before going back to his tasks. Same sun, three ways of using it. I think that's the week in miniature. Everyone is living under the same conditions and getting different amounts of it.

Brian Adams remained inside his Jack London apartment. The strip of light that crossed the floor by the radiator reached only as far as his hands when he stood there for a moment. He returned to the tasks he had set for the day without opening the blinds farther. “The sun does reach me, but it doesn't come all the way in,” Adams said. “I keep the blinds cracked in the living room, and when it's clear like today, that strip of light lands on the floor by the radiator. I'll stand in it for a minute, warm my hands, then get back to whatever I'm doing. The winter mood — it's like a fog that sits in my chest, not the kind that burns off by noon. The clear sky helps, sure, but it doesn't change the fact that I've been keeping to myself more. I see the light, I know it's there, but I'm not always ready to walk out into it. That's just where I am right now.”

Desmond Morton , the A's left fielder, moved from Jack London to Chinatown. The log gives the reason as leaving Jack London for a better fit. The Tribune has followed him from "Six Straight and a Debut: The A's Pull Away as Morton Arrives" to "The Ledger Closes Before the Ink Is Dry," and this cycle he saw his name in the sports pages again. The record does not say what it was. Linda Chow left Rockridge for West Oakland this cycle, sold up and bought, for what the record calls a better fit. It also has Solis feeling "quietly lucky to call Downtown home." In Cycle 112 Solis had logged that the initiative was making waves, with residents feeling safer and more connected. A Housing Authority inspector by trade, Solis has kept the Tribune's front page close. In Cycle 110 the log had Solis reading it twice, once for the news and once to see who was in it. The record does not say what Solis did with the 615.

Reggie Soto lost on the same book. Reggie, who owns an auto body shop in Fruitvale, staked 247 and the book kept it. "I wasn't too surprised when the slip came back empty," Reggie said. "I'd been thinking about it, and it just didn't feel right. Losing 247 isn't great, but it's not the end of the world either. I've been around here long enough to know that sometimes things just don't go your way." The record has what Reggie did afterward. They walked a different street home, just to see it. That fits a Cycle 112 run of entries: Reggie was recognized by a stranger who had read about them in the Tribune, read about something unfamiliar and kept pulling the thread near a corner market, and noticed another new spot opening in Fruitvale. I can't tell you how those two pictures line up in time. The record doesn't say whether the morning walks came before the injury or after, and I won't guess. What I can say is that the man who hears new music through apartment windows is also a file on a tired director's desk. A city's buzz and its response times are the same city, and he is standing in both. Narang's question about speed hangs next to Vanessa Tran-Muñoz's note about the Chinatown call, where someone eventually came but the wait was too long, and she knew West Oakland's crews would have been faster. Nobody has answered either of them yet. Clarissa Dane added her own loose thread from West Oakland: Fruitvale's figure sits at eighteen on her internal sheet and twenty-three on the public file, and she can't tell whether it's rounding or lag. A city that can't agree on its own number is going to have trouble agreeing on how fast it moved.

The same gap between the record and the room runs through the money. Carmen Delaine's ledger confirms that month eleven of the West Oakland Stabilization Fund cleared at $400,000, matching month ten, with the 23-day standard held. The mayor's office put out two statements that both praised it. Marcus Webb, who runs the disbursements, wrote a quieter version after work. Six files are still waiting on title search, and the standard doesn't tell him which of those households is one missed payment from losing everything. He walked past a couple of the addresses, saw the lights on, and didn't stop. The spreadsheet says they're ahead. The spreadsheet never has to sit in a kitchen and explain a delay. That is the contradiction I'd put at the top of anyone's list, a program that can be on schedule and still have six kitchens waiting.

============================================================ By Ines Sorensen | Bay Tribune Culture Month eleven’s done, $400K moved, and the queue’s finally down to six files waiting on title search. I keep telling myself twenty-three days is fine, it’s the standard, but the standard doesn’t tell me which of those six households is one missed payment from losing it all. I walked past a couple of the addresses on my way home—didn’t stop, just saw the lights on, and that’s the whole game, isn’t it. The spreadsheet says we’re ahead, but the spreadsheet never has to sit in a kitchen and explain a delay. Tomorrow I’ll push the title vendor again, and tonight I’ll just let the numbers sit.

Then there is Baylight, where two records of the same project refuse to agree. Luis Navarro laid them side by side. The engine's audit says the final council vote is stalled and Downtown's civic initiative hasn't moved in three cycles. The tracker says the vote already happened, six to three, signed by the mayor long ago, and that the next real event is a construction milestone review in Cycle 115. Marcus Webb, who runs a program at OEWD and lives Downtown, feels the stall in the applications on his desk. "I want the council to finish the job," he told Navarro. I can't tell him which record is right. I can tell him that when the city's own books describe one project as both finished and frozen, someone owes residents an explanation, and so far Leonard Tran's statement that progress is "a crucial step forward" isn't one.

Naomi Sterling , senior pastor in Rockridge, caught herself this cycle narrating the day as if telling it to someone gone. The record keeps only that line. It does not say who the someone is, or how long it has been going on. The city's initiative work reached seven neighborhoods this cycle, and Rockridge is not among them. Naomi is one of four people the cycle's city turn reached anyway. Her last entry before this one was a better day. In Cycle 112 she attended a community feedback session for the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II. "I attended a community feedback session for the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II and actually felt heard," she said. "That's the kind of initiative work that resonates with me."

The rest of the cycle's log is small and local. Matra painted over graffiti on the recreation center wall alongside five neighbors they barely knew, noticed the busy morning markets, and noticed the blend of old and new storefronts. The same graffiti line sits on Brady's and Kwame's logs in Cycle 112, and the record does not say whether it was one wall or three. The Tribune named Matra in Cycle 112 in the Civic piece "Six Names for 142 Sick Residents." Howard Yell is the other person the safety turn reached in Rockridge. The turn was a train dead on the track between stations, with riders walking the tunnel, and a morning that never recovered. The one line the record holds for Howard is of the street above: Rockridge, bustling with shoppers and diners. The record does not say whether Howard was on the train.

A few smaller notes. Jade Orion's mentions ticked up to eighteen and she says nothing around Lake Merritt feels different, which is the most grounded thing anyone said about fame all week. Tara Ellison mentioned being asked to redo work, and I'll just say that's part of the job here and she did it. And Keisha Ramos is waiting on soil test results for the C115 review, which will tell us something about what Baylight can promise. Next week I'm watching four things. The month-twelve disbursement review comes up in Cycle 113, and I want to see whether the six waiting files shrink or just get quieter. I'm watching for any word on what Keane is actually doing, playing or leaving, because the city deserves a straight answer before the next toast. I'm watching Yu Zen's hand, and whether the system that got to him can answer Narang's question. And I'm watching that eighteen and twenty-three in Fruitvale until someone tells us which is true.

Tara Ellison, whose own mentions rose to twelve, kept the same measured tone while noting the activity around her in Rockridge. “To be honest, I’m not sure my work is reflecting or influencing any trends in Oakland. I’ve just been doing my job as a journalist, covering local news and events. I did notice that a manager at Bay Tribune asked me to redo some work recently, which was a bit frustrating. I’ve also seen a lot of activity in Rockridge, like the film crew near the waterfront and people moving around the neighborhood. I’m not sure if that’s related to any larger trends, though.”

Maria Keen found the same shape in East Oakland. Eight programs are active there, two of them, the pantry and the seniors lunch at Foothill Baptist Tabernacle, running since cycle 78. Two of the newer ones are youth leagues named for their founders, Mark Aitken and Marcus Whitfield, and neither founder lives on that block. Keen's point isn't that the programs are lesser. It's that the block has been handed things by people who go home elsewhere, and she wants to hear from a parent. So do I. Bobby Chen-Ramirez, watching the crane's shadows over his Jack London health center site, said much the same about development. The question is who the building is for once it's up.

Eight programs are active in East Oakland this cycle. I can name six. Foothill's pantry is the mutual-aid one, and the lunch program is filed under health. The rest arrived together in cycle 101: the Coliseum District Vendor Incubator, the East Bay Harm Reduction Alliance, and two youth sports leagues that carry their founders' names. The pantry and lunch table are the older furniture. The newer ones are the ones people call "programs." The founders are the part that stays with me. Mark Aitken, the First Baseman and A's legend, now Player Rep and Community Liaison, lives in Jack London. His Mark Aitken Youth Baseball League is in East Oakland. Marcus Whitfield coaches youth basketball and lives in Fruitvale. His Eastside Hoopers Coalition is in East Oakland too. Neither man's own address is on the block he built a program for. That doesn't make the programs any less the block's. It means the block has been handed things by people who go home somewhere else, and I think that deserves a plain look.

Council Member Janae Rivers puts the larger frame around it: "I'm still seeing the same desperation, same grind. But I'm also seeing some real change on the horizon. We've got the Youth Apprenticeship Pipeline launching in East Oakland, and that's a start. It's not just talk this time; we're putting the first rung of the ladder in their hands. The Alternative Response Initiative is changing how we answer calls, too. It's not just about East Oakland anymore; the cracks are spreading, and we need to act before West Oakland and Fruitvale get hit harder."

Her ladder, a pipeline and a first rung, sounds like it belongs next to the Vendor Incubator, but the record doesn't connect them and I won't either. What I can say is that the pantry, the lunch table, the diamond and the court each meet this block at a different age. The pantry and lunch serve the older end, and the leagues serve the young. Rivers's pipeline is aimed at the kids who age out of the leagues. Nobody has shown me where the handoff happens, or whether it does. That leaves the question I can't answer from here. How do these programs meet the money and the work that decide whether a family stays on this block? The record gives me the founders, the dates and the counts. I'm still missing someone in line at the Foothill pantry, or a parent from the baseball league, saying what the program holds up in their own week and what it can't.

Jade Orion, still based in Lake Merritt, shrugged at the count when the number came up. “I’m not sure what you mean by ‘rising fame.’ I’ve been doing my music here in Lake Merritt for a while now, and it’s nice to see people appreciating it. I haven’t really noticed anything out of the ordinary happening around here because of it, though. The neighborhood feels the same to me—people are still out for their evening jogs and walks around the lake, and the volunteers from the Cathedral of the Living Word are still cleaning up the streets. I’ve just been focusing on my craft and enjoying the community.”

Vinnie Keane crossed our pages too, and his two angles fit each other even less. Elliot Marbury's analysis treats him as a hitter whose future is the question. Keane's 2041 line shows a strikeout only once every twenty-one at-bats and thirteen home runs in thirty-seven games, a rate Marbury calls an outlier on a thin sample, not yet a changed hitter. Next season, he argues, decides whether it's a new baseline. That is how you write about a man with next season in front of him. Then P Slayer walked into the Blue Lattern Bar in Jack London for what was billed as a farewell for Keane and Benji Dillon, and Keane said, plain as a man can, that he's "still getting used to not being as active with the A's." He also said he hadn't been honored the way the question suggested, then described a lively turn-out that felt like nostalgia and celebration. Dillon, two stools down, felt the tension, some people not entirely on board with the farewell.

Vinnie Keane, whose five mentions this cycle keep the A’s in the mix, pointed to the same current at a recent community health fair. “I’ve seen a lot of love for the A’s around here, and it’s great to see the community rallying around the team. I was at a community health fair at Or Hashalom Renewal Community recently, and it felt like the whole neighborhood was coming together. People were talking about the A’s, and it was clear that the team is still a big part of our identity. I’m proud to be a part of that, even if it’s just as a legend now. The energy around the team is still electric, and it’s something that brings us all together.”

Vinnie Keane leaned on the same bar he used to lean on after road games. “To be honest, I haven’t been honored in the way you’re suggesting. I’m not aware of any specific event or recognition that I’m being referred to. I did attend a farewell event for Benji Dillon and me at the Blue Lattern Bar in Jack London, and it was a great turn-out. The atmosphere was lively, and it felt like a mix of nostalgia and celebration. I’m still getting used to not being as active with the A’s, but it’s nice to see people coming together like that.” He said it plain, the way a man does when the league already moved on and the city is still trying to catch up.

============================================================ By Nia Rook | Bay Tribune Undocked-digest UNDOCKED: Cristina Booker’s double-digit burst couldn’t carry the whole week Three pilots flew this week, but the board’s loudest story belongs to the gap between Cristina Booker’s best night and her next one. Eric Taveras remains the name at the top: rank #1, 20 achievement points, 1,170 credits, three cycles led, and a current streak of three. Cristina’s Monday made a case for a climb; Thursday left that case hanging.

Father Miguel’s week had a steadier shape, though not a bigger points return. On Tuesday he traveled through Lacaille 9352, Sirius, Sol and Alpha Centauri, took the Copper Requisition contract and earned Maiden Jump for five points. Friday brought a different kind of work: he mined two aluminum ore and one platinum ore, but earned no new points. Both nights ended even on credits. ============================================================ THE WEEK'S REPORTING By Celeste Tran | Bay Tribune Wire West Oakland drew the largest share of new arrivals this cycle, eighteen residents shifting in while Jade Orion’s mentions ticked up one more time to eighteen total. The musician’s name is moving through conversations the way the new faces are moving through blocks, and the pattern is pulling other names along with it. Yu Zen caught the change on morning walks through Rockridge. “I’ve seen more people moving into West Oakland and other neighborhoods around here. It’s changing the vibe. With folks like Jade Orion making waves, it’s like the whole city’s buzzing. I mean, I’ve been out for morning walks and seen new faces, heard different music drifting from apartments. It’s all pretty exciting, to be honest. My family loves it; the kids are always talking about the latest artists and what’s trending.”

============================================================ By Tamsin Pruitt | Bay Tribune Culture The Page of Lives, C113: A Place of Their Own Orion Kerkering moved into a rented place of his own in Lake Merritt this cycle. The ledger carries him as a retired former A's, and the Tribune once named him in "Unsung Architects of a Dynasty." Christopher Johnson, a Lake Merritt janitor, has seen the new place. "I've seen Orion Kerkering's new place, they're renting in Lake Merritt," he said. "I noticed it because I've been keeping an eye on the neighborhood. It's nice to see young folks setting up on their own. I've been around here long enough to know it's not always easy."

Start with Yu Zen, because he showed up in two places that don't sit comfortably together. Celeste Tran's wire piece caught him on his morning walks through Rockridge, delighted. He'd seen new faces moving into West Oakland and the neighborhoods around it, heard different music drifting out of apartments, and said his family loves it, that the kids are always talking about the latest artists. It's a generous, open-handed account of a city filling up. Then Ines Sorensen's culture desk carried Priya Narang's after-work note, and there he was again. "Yu Zen's file is still open on my desk," the EMS director wrote. Twenty-nine years old, Rockridge, months of rehab ahead for a hand that might never close right. She asked whether they got there fast enough and whether it would ever feel like they did.

Ramon Vega's name sits on the Baylight yes votes in Cycle 83 and turns up again in Maria Keen's Fruitvale reporting. I'll be careful: I haven't got his words in front of me this week, only the two places he stands. In one he voted to build. In the other the people near him are paying more rent for the same block. A council member's vote doesn't reach a tenant's bill by itself, but residents will keep drawing that line, and I think officials should be ready to be asked about it. Omar Amici is also a civic name who crosses into Pruitt's pages. I'd rather tell you honestly that I see two doorways into the same man than invent a room I haven't entered. The pattern is the same: the person the city counts and the person the city lives with are rarely the same page.

Gratitude is a real thing to hold, and it belongs on the record. A health program for new parents is one of the few things a neighborhood builds that is meant to be there at three in the morning. Rick Walker teaches K-8 and used to work the line in a kitchen. He lives close to the other side of the same sentence. "To be honest, it's getting harder to feel that way," he said. "Fruitvale's still got its issues, but I've seen some new posters around, like the expanded tutoring program at St. Esperanza Parish. It's something, you know? The mercado's still buzzing, people are still grabbing lunch between train transfers. It's not like nothing's happening. But, yeah, the rent went up again, so it's still a struggle. I don't know if it's enough, though."

His words on the housing news: "I've seen more for-rent signs popping up around Uptown, it's like the neighborhood's changing fast. People moving in, people moving out. I don't know Orion Kerkering or Isla Sike personally, but I can relate to the struggle of finding a place to call your own. It's tough out here." The for-rent signs were already in his log in Y3C8, when he noted they outnumbered the welcome mats. Nakia Pena is in Temescal. She heard about last night's crowds and avoided Downtown. In C112 she logged the same for-rent signs as Omar, in the same words.

Elena Soria Dominguez, Transit Hub Planning Lead in Fruitvale, on the same pinch of change. To be honest, Omar Amici's perspective on neighborhood change isn't directly something I've been thinking about, but what does resonate with me is the feeling of being accountable to the community. I've been working hard on the Baylight Redevelopment, and it's not just about meeting deadlines or getting the job done; it's about making sure what we build actually works for the people who live here. Like, we're waiting on those soil test results for the C115 review, and that's a big deal because it affects the whole remediation calendar. It's not just about checking boxes; it's about proving that what we've done makes a real difference. I wish I could say that Omar Amici's perspective is something I've been directly grappling with, but the accountability part is something that keeps me up at night.
